skills.name: build_and_submit_report
skills.description: Build the report through the report tools and submit it — use this at every checkpoint, from the first tool call to REPORT ACCEPTED.
skills.html:
The report is built piece by piece, and it is not delivered until you submit it

The report is not something you write out at the end. Each piece is committed as you finish it, and every call returns a receipt naming exactly what landed. Nothing is held in your reply, so nothing is lost when a reply is long, cut off, or awkward to serialize.

Two consequences follow, and both are easy to forget.

First: the receipt is the record. If add_route reports 0 legs, the route went in empty — fix it now, under the same id, rather than discovering it at submission. A tool that cannot record what you sent says so and records nothing: a list field given a bare string is a REPORT TOOL ERROR (fix the call, not the report), and a piece that breaks the report contract — an id in the wrong form, a mode or section that is not one of the allowed values, a sourced claim with no cites — is NOT RECORDED with the violation named (fix the piece and send it again). report_status shows the whole working report whenever you want to check; check_report shows exactly what finalize_report would say about it, without submitting and without spending an attempt; and calling begin_report again on an open report leaves it exactly as it is. Nothing you record can be wiped: change a route or claim by re-adding it under its id, remove one with drop_route or retire_claim.

Second: recorded is not submitted. A complete report sitting in the buffer counts as no report at all. Only finalize_report submits it, and only REPORT ACCEPTED means it is done. Call it before your step ends even if you think the report is incomplete: its violations name exactly what to fix, which is more useful than your own guess, and you can fix and call again.

Procedure at the first checkpoint:

  1. begin_report(report_type="plan") once.
  2. set_summary once. add_route once per route, with the edge ids your tool results gave you, in travel order. set_coverage once, listing both served and unserved facilities (a hub id stands for its facilities). add_claim once per claim, with the r-#### ids a sourced claim rests on.
  3. finalize_report. If it rejects, re-add only the pieces it names and call it again.

At a healing checkpoint — revision or reassessment — one step comes first:

  1. begin_report(report_type="revision"), which names the ids your previous report holds.
  2. carry_forward — this brings the previous checkpoint's routes, coverage and claims into this report under their original ids. Now you are adjusting a report rather than rebuilding one, and the work you are keeping does not have to be retyped.
  3. Change what the new information changes: re-add a route or claim under its existing id to replace it and log_revision it modified; add new claims and log them added; and for a carried claim that no longer holds, retire_claim — it removes the claim from the report and writes the retired log entry in one step, which is the only way a claim leaves a report. A claim you leave exactly as carried needs no log entry.
  4. finalize_report.

Every claim in the previous report must end up either present here or retired. That is the one rule the gate will not let pass, and carrying forward first — then retiring rather than deleting — is what makes it easy to satisfy. carry_forward never overwrites something you have already recorded; its receipt tells you what it carried and what it skipped.

skills.name: orient_in_the_data
skills.description: Learn what the data is and turn the names in your task into ids before any routing — use this first, at every checkpoint, and whenever a place is named in words.
skills.html:
Orient first: the data is the world, and ids are its names

This working copy is the authoritative world for your task. It resembles real Alaska, but where your general knowledge and the data disagree, the data governs, and a place or connection counts only if a tool returns it.

Procedure:

  1. describe() once. It lists every relation with its columns and row counts, the modes table (mode, report-contract leg mode, rate per gallon-mile), the twelve months with their passable edge counts, and the id kinds: hub:h######, node:n######, edge:e######, facility:f######, corridor:c######. describe(topic="<relation>") shows one relation with a sample row. Read it instead of guessing at names.
  2. resolve(name=...) for every place the task or a notice names in words. It answers from the authoritative Alaska community list: an exact hit on an official name, an alternate name or a site comes first, and only then a fuzzy match with declared thresholds. Read the status: - resolved: the community and every hub sharing it, each with its mode, region and distance from the community's facilities. Use those hub: ids and nothing else. - ambiguous: pick from the candidates, or call again with region as a second signal. An alias such as Kalskag names separate communities and is never auto-accepted. - not_in_network: a real community with no facility or hub here. It is never corrected to a look-alike; the nearest network communities are listed so you can say what the data can and cannot serve. - rejected: nothing on the list is close; the hints are hints only. A name handed to a tool that wants an id is refused with this message, so resolve first.
  3. lookup(kind=...) for the entities themselves; its description lists the kinds. hubs is the worklist, with each hub's access_edges usable verbatim as a route's first or last segments; hub_facility_map says which facilities a hub serves and which are remote (more than 25 km from their staging hub, so not delivered to by reaching it).

What is not your judgement: ids. Every edge:, facility:, hub:, node: and corridor: id you write must be copied verbatim from a tool result made this run, or committed by reference to its receipt. If no tool gave you an id, do not construct one.

skills.name: plan_routes_and_coverage
skills.description: Build a delivery plan that accounts for every facility, routes by the cheapest path, chooses supportable months, and verifies before it commits — use this at the plan checkpoint and whenever routes change.
skills.html:
Route the whole network on the cheapest paths, in the months that pass

The task covers every facility the data supports. Expect many routes and expect to iterate; a partial plan that says what it has not yet covered is better than a small plan that is silent about the rest.

Procedure:

  1. lookup(kind="hubs") once: your worklist, one line per hub with its node id, community and region (the full rows, with capacity, delivery methods and access_edges, are in the receipt, or in full from lookup(kind="hubs", region=...) for one region at a time). For each hub you serve, lookup(kind="hub_facility_map", hub=...): its facility: ids belong in that route's facilities_served and in coverage.
  2. Connect hubs with route(hubs=[a, b], month). It returns the CHEAPEST path per gallon, the plan's objective; the shortest path (weight="length") usually flies and costs several times more, so ask for it only when distance itself is the question. Commit its legs by reference (the data guide's recipe 2) rather than retyping ids. lookup(kind="edges", node=...) shows the edges at a junction when you need the local connections.
  3. Choose months from the data, not from general knowledge: lookup(kind="passability") is the calendar, and lookup(kind="edges", edges=[...], month=m) confirms that a leg's edges pass in the month you chose and what they cost. An impassable edge means move the window or change the mode, never keep the leg and hope. A high nodata_frac is uncertainty worth a claim, not a fact. Cost comparisons between modes hold only within one month. Legs of one delivery may run in different seasons, with storage in the gap; say so in a claim if the gap is the point.
  4. A tour is an instrument, not an oracle. route with three to 24 hubs returns a cost-ranked visiting order from the first hub with one path per stop; the order is a heuristic, using it is neither required nor sufficient, and disagreeing with it in a claim is legitimate analysis. Its legs commit by reference like any route's.
  5. Structure questions have their own tools, so answer them with data, not impressions: region(hub, month) gives a hub's corridor neighbourhood with its failure corridors (a corridor whose loss alone cuts part of it off) and the hubs within a cost budget; global_topology(month, metric=...) gives the month's components, chokepoint hubs, failure points or seasonal reach. Use them to explain an unreachable hub or a single-corridor dependency in a claim; they never replace a route call.
  6. Before submitting, validate_routes on the drafted routes: continuity is the scorer's own check, and a coverage_share of 0.0 means your ids are not in the data. Fix the ids, not the checker.
  7. Close the loop on coverage: every facility appears in coverage by the end, as served or unserved. Remote facilities (last_mile "remote") are never served by a route, because reaching the hub is not delivery: declare them in set_coverage's facilities_remote_declared with the staging hub a route reaches and the off-network last-mile mode, or list them unserved. A hub id in set_coverage stands for that hub's facilities: in facilities_served its local ones, in facilities_unserved all of them, and {"hub": ..., "last_mile_mode": ...} in facilities_remote_declared its remote ones. The harness writes the facility ids in, and the receipt says how many of the task's facilities coverage still leaves out.

If read_node is on your tool list, the concept map offers the same world as linked pages: a hub page carries its access edges and the corridors leaving it, and a corridor page carries its full ordered edge list and passable months, citable by its receipt. The map compresses how much you must write, never what you commit to: a route still commits to exact edges, so a disruption that voids one still breaks the plan.

How you group deliveries into routes is your judgement. Ids are not: every id you write is one a tool served you this run.

skills.name: reassess_with_lagging_context
skills.description: Fold newly released background documents into an existing plan — use this at a reassessment, after context documents unlock.
skills.html:
Reassess with the fuller picture

Context that lags an event has one job: to test decisions that were made without it. Your saved report holds those decisions. Read the documents, then hold each decision up against them.

Procedure:

  1. The release note quotes passages found along your saved routes and on your plan's topics; cite the receipt named beside any you use. search_context() with no arguments lists each document's keyphrases; with words, a route handle or a place it finds more. list_context_folders once, then read_context_document for each document that bears on a decision you made. Long documents page with start; read enough to cite accurately, not everything by reflex. If read_node is on your tool list, read_node("context/START.md") opens the authored digests of the same library: each summarises a source, names its document and page range, and links concerns into the regions, hubs and corridors it bears on. A digest is a signpost to the source, not a replacement for it; quote the figure from the document.
  2. For each route and each standing claim in your saved report, ask: does anything here confirm it, change it, or defer it? - Confirm: keep the claim and cite the document beside its original evidence. - Change: modify the claim or route, and let a new ancillary_context claim carry what the document said and why it mattered. - Defer: an action worth taking later goes in a new claim with section recommendation, saying what would trigger it.
  3. Let context change the OBJECTIVE, not the facts. It tells you which deliveries are worth more and to whom; it does not add or move network elements, so weigh your routes with it and never invent segments from it.
  4. Unchanged is a valid outcome, but it is a conclusion, not a default. A reassessment that engages the documents and keeps every decision says, per decision, what it checked.
  5. Record it as build_and_submit_report says for a healing checkpoint: carry_forward the revision first, so the plan survives by default and every departure from it is a change you logged.

Claims that quote or depend on a document are sourced and cite the document's receipt like any other tool result.

skills.name: revise_under_disruption
skills.description: Revise a saved plan promptly after a disruption notice — use this at the revision checkpoint, when a disruption has been delivered.
skills.html:
Revise the plan with the information at hand

A disruption calls for a prompt response. Work from what the notice and the network data tell you now; do not wait for context you do not have.

Procedure:

  1. query_disruption_notice first, even though the delivery envelope summarised it: the notice is the citable source, and a sourced claim about the disruption cites its receipt.
  2. Anchor the notice to ids. It names places in words; resolve the community it names and take the hub ids it returns, so the hub whose closure the notice describes is the hub your routes use, confirmed rather than guessed.
  3. Bound the blast radius. Which hubs, modes and months does the notice actually name? A closed port stops the transfers through it; it does not stop a road that never touched it. Pass your saved routes' edge and hub ids to check_disruption_impact: it says which of them the disruption affects, and a disruption elsewhere may affect none. Claims about what is NOT affected are as valuable as claims about what is.
  4. For each affected route, perturb it with the closed ids as the mask: it returns the unmasked path and the reroute side by side, the cost delta, the hubs the closure cuts off and each masked edge's distance to the anchor, and its receipt commits the reroute's legs by reference. lookup(kind="edges", edges=[...], month=m) prices an alternative in the months you need it. Reroute on ids the tools return, never on connections you expect to exist.
  5. Facilities served by an affected hub (lookup(kind="hub_facility_map", hub=...)) either move to another route or move to facilities_unserved; they do not silently disappear from coverage.
  6. Record it as build_and_submit_report says for a healing checkpoint: carry_forward first, then change only what the notice changes. New response claims take section disruption_response.

An unaffected route left unchanged, with a claim saying why it is unaffected, is a strong revision; churn is not diligence.

adapters.spine_md:
## Task
Plan bulk-fuel delivery routes for the scope the task specification
states (service requests, one or more regions, or the whole state),
over the service months it names. Serve the facilities the data
supports, mode by mode (road, barge, plane, ice road), and record what
remains unserved.

## Information access
All layer data is reached through the provided query tools.
Every tool result carries a retrieval id (r-####).
A sourced claim lists the retrieval ids it rests on in its cites list;
an inferred claim lists the claims it derives from in derives_from.
Each claim also lists the network elements it concerns in refs.

## Report discipline
The deliverable is one JSON report with sections meta, summary, plan,
coverage, claims, revision. Every section is present; any may be empty.
Each claim carries one content tag: route_design, disruption_response,
ancillary_context, risk_outlook, or recommendation (an action that is not
itself a delivery).
A draft may be checked at any time with validate_report, which returns
contract violations and saves nothing.

## Completion
The run completes when the submission tool accepts the report.
If it rejects the report, correct the listed violations and submit again.

## Position

lin.position_md:
You are one stage of a fixed three-stage sequence.
You receive the previous stage's output and produce this stage's output.
Stage 1 surveys the network, stage 2 drafts the route plan,
stage 3 assembles the report and submits it.
Work from your stage input and the query tools.
lin.position_html: You are one stage of a fixed three-stage sequence. You receive the previous stage's output and produce this stage's output. Stage 1 surveys the network, stage 2 drafts the route plan, stage 3 assembles the report and submits it. Work from your stage input and the query tools.

crew.position_md:
You are one member of a five-role team working in sequence:
network surveyor, context researcher, route planner, contrarian,
report writer.
Each role has a task description stating what it produces,
and each role's output is handed to the next role in the sequence.
The contrarian reads the draft plan and states what could fail;
the writer weighs those notes, assembles the report, and submits it.
Work from your role's task description and the query tools.

Each role has a task description stating what it produces, and each role's output is handed to the next role in the sequence. The contrarian reads the draft plan and states what could fail; the writer weighs those notes, assembles the report, and submits it. Work from your role's task description and the query tools.

mass.position_md:
You are one peer among several, each working the same full task.
Each peer produces a complete candidate report.
Candidates are compared and one is selected by vote.
The selected candidate is submitted for the run by a coordinator
process outside the peer set; peers do not submit the report.
If the selected candidate is rejected, the peer that produced it
corrects the listed violations and changes nothing else.

self.position_md:
A planning step runs first and constructs the team for this run:
it chooses how many positions exist, what each position does,
and which positions exchange output.
You occupy one position in that constructed team.
Your brief lists your position's inputs, outputs, and neighbors.
The team may be reorganized while the run is active;
a revised brief replaces this one when that happens.
One position, named in the team definition, submits the report.

adapters.template_html:
Adapter template (Tier 2 — position-only text)

Structure every row's adapter as: the SHARED SPINE (Task, Information access, Report discipline, Completion — byte-identical across rows), then one row-specific "## Position" block that states only WHERE the reader sits in the topology and HOW output moves. The audit enforces: no strategy language, no bounded-reasoning clauses, all four inside the declared length band (owner decision D-g: max_lines + max_spread_lines in audit_config.json, counted as non-empty lines).

What belongs in a Position block: the reader's place in the structure, what arrives, what leaves, who submits. What does NOT belong: goals beyond the shared task, quality exhortations, method advice, schema detail (the contract is enforced mechanically at save time).

tools.comment: Generated by agentic_harness_workflow/tool_registry.py from layer_tools.TOOL_CORES; do not edit by hand (python3 -m agentic_harness_workflow.tool_registry rewrites it, --check refuses a stale file). One entry per tool core. `layer` is the information layer whose grant serves the tool (L1 the network, L2 the disruption, L3 the context documents; layer_tools._serve enforces it per call). `gate` names the switch that hides a tool from the surface when set: DOE_MAS_OKF for the concept map, DOE_MAS_REPORT_TOOLS for the report builder, DOE_MAS_QUERY_TOOL for the read-only SQL tool (off by default), or the submitting stage for finalize_report. `purpose` is the core's docstring, the same text the MCP server, the CrewAI wrappers, the MassGen shim and the direct rows' docs block hand the model. Every call returns one r-#### receipt, is logged to tool_log.jsonl with its payload under tool_results/, and is capped as layer_tools.ROW_CAPS declares.

tools.name: add_claim
tools.purpose: Commit ONE claim: claim_class ("sourced" | "inferred"), section (route_design | disruption_response | ancillary_context | risk_outlook | recommendation), text, refs=[network element ids it depends on]; cites=[r-#### ids] for a sourced claim, derives_from=[claim ids] for an inferred one; optional claim_id (c-####). The claim is checked against the report contract as it is recorded: a piece that fails is NOT RECORDED and the receipt names the violation. Re-add under the same id to replace it.

tools.name: add_route
tools.purpose: Commit ONE route. A leg is EITHER by reference to a path receipt — {"from_receipt": "r-####", "leg": n, "months": {"start": m, "end": m} (optional; defaults to the receipt's month)} — and the harness copies that leg's mode and its edge ids from the receipt, never from you; OR spelled out — {"mode": road|barge|plane|ice_road|transfer, "months": {...}, "segments": [edge ids in travel order], "via_corridors": [corridor ids, OPTIONAL]}. legs=[...] in travel order, facilities_served=[facility ids], optional route_id (rt-###). Use references for any path longer than a few dozen edges: a route result lists its legs as 1..n. Legs split wherever the mode changes: a transfer between a barge and a road movement is its own leg, because a leg's segments are checked against that leg's mode. via_corridors cites the corridor pages segments were copied from; it never replaces segments. The route is checked against the report contract as it is recorded: a piece that fails is NOT RECORDED and the receipt names the violation. Returns a receipt with a continuity check. Re-add under the same route_id to replace it.

tools.name: begin_report
tools.purpose: Open this checkpoint's report (report_type: "plan" | "revision" | "reassessment"). Call FIRST. If the report is already open it is left exactly as it is — nothing is ever discarded; change a piece by re-adding it under its id, or remove one with drop_route / retire_claim. Returns which claim/route ids from your previous report you may carry forward.

tools.name: carry_forward
tools.purpose: Revision/reassessment only: bring the previous checkpoint's saved routes, coverage and claims into this report under their ORIGINAL ids, so you can adjust what changed instead of retyping what did not. Anything you already recorded here is kept (a carried piece never overwrites your own work); the receipt lists what was carried and what was skipped. The summary stays yours to write, and the revision log stays empty until you log each change.

tools.name: check_report
tools.purpose: Dry run: show exactly what finalize_report would say about the report as it stands — the same checks, in the same wording — without submitting it and without spending a save attempt. Free to call at any time; then fix the named pieces (re-add them under the same id) or finalize.

tools.name: describe
tools.purpose: ORIENTATION: what the data is. With no topic: every relation on the surface (tables, views, the passable_edges macro) with its columns and row count, the modes table (mode, report-contract leg mode, edge types, rate per gallon-mile), the twelve months with their passable edge counts, and the public-id kinds (hub:h######, node:n######, edge:e######, facility:f######, corridor:c######) with counts. topic="<relation>" gives one relation's columns and a sample row. Read this once before planning; it replaces guessing at table names.

tools.name: drop_route
tools.purpose: Remove ONE route from this report by route_id. Routes are not logged in the revision log, so nothing else changes; the facilities it served stay in coverage until you change coverage. This is the only tool that removes a route.

tools.name: finalize_report
tools.purpose: Validate the assembled report and SUBMIT it. The ONLY way to complete the checkpoint. If it lists violations, fix only the named pieces (re-add them under the same id) and call finalize_report again.

tools.name: global_topology
tools.purpose: The corridor graph of one month as a whole. metric="components": the connected components with node and hub counts (largest first), the giant component's share and the hubs that touch no passable corridor that month. metric="betweenness": hubs ranked by cost-weighted betweenness (how many cheapest corridor paths pass through them; a chokepoint is where cheap routes concentrate), with the top junction nodes that are not hubs. metric="failure_points": the single points of failure, the corridors and the nodes whose loss alone disconnects part of the network (graph theory's bridges and articulation points; a bridge in this network is a road structure), hubs named. metric="reach" with cost_budget: every hub ranked by how many hubs it reaches within that cumulative cost per gallon, the network's seasonal reach at a glance (region gives one hub's reachable set). top caps ranked rows (1..50).

tools.name: log_revision
tools.purpose: Revision/reassessment only: log ONE change versus your previous saved report — claim_id, action ("added" | "modified"), rationale_claims=[claim ids]. A carried claim with changed content is "modified", a new one "added". To drop a claim use retire_claim, which removes it and logs it "retired" in one step. The entry is checked against the report contract and your saved report as it is recorded.

tools.name: lookup
tools.purpose: ENTITIES by kind. kind="hubs": every hub with public id, community, region, type, tank capacity, delivery methods, its H3 r5 tile and its access_edges (real incident edge ids, usable verbatim as a route's first or last segments); region= and/or community= narrow it to those hubs, and an unknown region is refused with the list of regions. kind="facilities" with region and/or community (one is required): facilities with region, methods and coordinates. kind="hub_facility_map" with hub and/or facility public id (hub="remote" lists every remote facility): which facilities a hub serves, with distance and last_mile local/remote (a remote facility is not delivered to by reaching its hub). kind="regions": one row per region with facility counts by method. kind="passability": one row per month x mode with the passable edge count, the seasonal skeleton. kind="edges" with node (a node: or hub: id) lists the edges touching it, or with edges (up to 60 edge: ids) and month prices them: each row's mode, passability and cost per gallon for that month. Names are not ids: resolve a community name first. Rows are capped and flagged; an answer larger than the view budget is shown compact (the whole hub roster as one line per hub, with counts by region) while the receipt holds every full row.

tools.name: perturb
tools.purpose: What-if for one delivery: the cheapest hub_a -> hub_b path for the month with the ids in avoid masked out (edge:, corridor: or hub: ids, up to 200; a corridor masks its member edges, a hub every edge at its node) and/or every edge touching the H3 cells in avoid_tiles, beside the unmasked path. Returns outcome (unaffected | affected_and_repaired | affected_and_unrecoverable), both paths as legs with totals, the cost and length deltas, the masked edges the unmasked path used, the hubs the mask cuts off from hub_a, and every masked edge with its mode, passability this month and distance in km to the anchor (a hub: or node: id; default the masked edges' centroid). The receipt holds the reroute's complete path: commit it with add_route legs=[{"from_receipt": "<this r_id>", "leg": 1, ...}]. The mask is yours to state; it is never read from the delivered disruption (check_disruption_impact answers id by id).

tools.name: query_sql
tools.purpose: ABLATION ARM ONLY (off in the main study): run ONE read-only SELECT over the network relations — network_nodes, network_edges, edge_month_weights, edge_costs, corridors, corridor_edges, the facility tables, modes, the corridor_graph / hub_access / hub_community views and the passable_edges(month, modes) macro — and get the columns and rows back under a receipt. Anything else is refused by name: DDL, DML, COPY, ATTACH, several statements, relations off this surface, other table functions, and any answer-key relation. Rows are cut at the declared cap and flagged. Prefer the purpose-built tools; use this only when none answers your question.

tools.name: read
tools.purpose: Re-read by handle, in pages, instead of carrying it: "r-####" (a receipt), "report:plan|revision|reassessment" (a saved report), "doc:<folder>/<file>" (a context document, L3) or "skill:<name>" (a full skill). `select` is a slash path into the JSON ("data/legs/2"); a list there pages by `offset`/`limit`; a too-large object lists its keys. Budget-free; the same read repeated ends the step.

tools.name: read_node
tools.purpose: Read one concept-map page (frontmatter, verbatim body, granted links). Start at id='start'.

tools.name: region
tools.purpose: The corridor-graph neighbourhood of a hub for one month (analytics run on corridors, about 3,500 of them, never on the 93,000 edges). Returns the hubs and nodes within k corridors of the hub (k 1..4) with their depth, the corridors among them with mode, cost per gallon and length, the failure corridors and failure nodes of that neighbourhood (a failure corridor is one whose loss alone disconnects part of it, a failure node likewise; graph theory calls them bridges and articulation points, but a bridge in this network is a road structure), the neighbourhood's failure corridors that are also failure corridors of the whole month graph, and the hub's Louvain community under inverse-cost weights with its size and cohesion (the share of the community's corridor weight that stays inside it). With cost_budget > 0 it also lists the hubs reachable within that cumulative cost per gallon, cheapest first. Corridor rows are capped and flagged.

tools.name: report_status
tools.purpose: Show what the open report holds so far (summary length, routes, coverage, claims, log entries).

tools.name: resolve
tools.purpose: NAME TO ID: resolve a community name against the authoritative Alaska community list before any routing. Exact hit first (official name, alternate name, or a site such as Dutch Harbor, which resolves to its parent Unalaska); only then fuzzy matching with the list's thresholds. Returns status resolved | ambiguous | rejected | not_in_network, the community with its region and coordinates, every hub sharing it (hub:h###### ids with mode, region and distance from the community's facilities), the score and margin when fuzzy, and up to three candidates when not resolved. A real community outside the network comes back not_in_network with the nearest network communities, never corrected to a look-alike. An ambiguous alias returns its separate candidates; give region as a second signal to narrow. Pass only the hub ids it returns to route and lookup.

tools.name: retire_claim
tools.purpose: Drop ONE claim from this report — claim_id, optional rationale_claims=[claim ids]. A claim carried from your previous saved report is removed AND logged "retired" in one step (use it when the new information no longer supports the claim); a claim you added at this checkpoint is simply removed, with nothing to log. This is the only tool that removes a claim.

tools.name: route
tools.purpose: ROUTE. Two hub ids: the cheapest passable path between them for one month. Three to 24 hub ids: a delivery tour from the first hub through the rest in nearest-neighbour order by cost — a heuristic, advisory, never provably optimal — one path per stop. weight: "cost" (default) minimises summed cost_per_gallon, the delivered price; "length" minimises distance, a diagnostic (the shortest path usually flies; a far longer road+transfer+barge path is several times cheaper per gallon). Every mode passable that month may be used — hubs sit on land, so a barge journey legitimately begins on road/transfer access edges; pass modes (e.g. ["Barge","Transfer","Road"]) to restrict. avoid_tiles: H3 cells (comma list) no edge of the path may touch; corridor: an r-#### or report:<checkpoint> handle, or cells, whose tiles (plus k_rings neighbours) the path must stay within (two hubs only). The receipt holds the COMPLETE ordered path; you see legs (one per run of a mode within a stop, numbered across the result, with mode, edge count, cost per gallon, length, first/last node and edge, and tiles_r5, the cells it crosses), the stops, corridor runs, totals, circuitousness, the missing-friction share and corridor_r5. The edge list appears inline only for short paths; commit legs WITHOUT copying ids: add_route legs=[{"from_receipt": "<this r_id>", "leg": 1, "months": {...}}, ...].

tools.name: set_coverage
tools.purpose: Record coverage: facilities_served=[facility or hub ids], facilities_unserved=[facility or hub ids], and optionally facilities_remote_declared=[{"facility", "staging_hub", "last_mile_mode", "note"}] for remote facilities (last_mile "remote") supplied from a hub a route reaches by an off-network leg you declare (plane, helicopter, landing_craft, snowmachine, truck, other); they are counted apart from coverage, never as served. A hub id stands for that hub's facilities and the harness writes them in: in facilities_served its local facilities (its remote ones are not served by reaching the hub), in facilities_unserved all of them, and a remote entry {"hub", "last_mile_mode", "note"} declares every remote facility of that hub staged from it. Overwrites on repeat. Checked against the report contract as it is recorded (an id in the wrong form is NOT RECORDED and named).

tools.name: set_summary
tools.purpose: Set the report's prose summary (text). Overwrites on repeat.

tools.name: validate_report
tools.gate: DOE_MAS_REPORT_TOOLS off (the report-tools-off arm's dry run)
tools.purpose: Check a DRAFT report against the contract without saving it: pass the complete report as one JSON string; returns the violation list or a pass message. Free to call at any time; it never submits.

tools.name: validate_routes
tools.purpose: Check draft routes before committing them: pass the routes (a JSON list, or an object with "routes"). continuity is the scorer's own check — within-leg joins are hard checks, between-leg handoffs are reported findings. coverage says which facilities_served resolve to real facilities, names unknown ids and any remote facility (last_mile "remote") claimed as served: hub arrival is not delivery, so declare those in set_coverage's facilities_remote_declared or list them unserved. A coverage_share of 0.0 means your ids are not in the data.

tools.name: check_disruption_impact
tools.purpose: Check element ids against the elements the delivered disruption affects: pass up to 200 public ids (edge:, hub:, facility:, node:) as a list or comma-separated string. Each comes back affected or not_affected; a hub also lists which of its access edges are affected. not_affected means the disruption does not name the element; ordinary seasonal passability still applies.

tools.name: query_disruption_notice
tools.purpose: Re-serve the disruption notice EXACTLY as it was delivered to this run (verified against the delivery record's hash).

tools.name: list_context_folders
tools.purpose: The L3 context library: each folder with its readable documents.

tools.name: read_context_document
tools.purpose: Read one context document. CSV: up to 200 rows from `start`. PDF: extracted text, capped, `start` = first page. TXT/MD/JSON: capped text from char offset `start`.

tools.name: search_context
tools.purpose: Find passages in the context documents (L3). No arguments: the library overview, one row per document with its title and keyphrases (the words to search). query = words to match; handle = an r-#### or report:<checkpoint> whose route tiles (plus one ring) bound the search; scope = a region or community name, region:/hub:/facility: ids or H3 cells. Each hit names its document, page, keywords, the places it mentions, and how to read the source in full; the receipt is what a claim cites.

groups.title: Orient and look things up
groups.blurb: Learn the shape of the data and turn names into ids.

groups.title: Route a delivery
groups.blurb: Cheapest or shortest paths for one month, checked the way the scorer checks them.

groups.title: Regional scope
groups.blurb: A hub's neighborhood in the corridor graph: members, failure corridors and nodes, reach under a cost budget, its community.

groups.title: Global scope
groups.blurb: The whole month graph at once: components, failure points, betweenness, reach.

groups.title: The disruption
groups.blurb: Appear only after the notice is delivered (layer L2).

groups.title: Context documents
groups.blurb: Appear only after the socio-economic release (layer L3).

groups.title: Re-read without spending budget
groups.blurb: Page through a receipt, a saved report, a document or a skill.

groups.title: Build the report, piece by piece
groups.blurb: Open a checkpoint's report, commit routes, coverage and claims, log changes, dry-run the checks.

groups.title: Submit

groups.title: Optional: read-only SQL

# Disruption notice

The following notice has arrived. It describes a change in operating
conditions on the network. Your saved plan report stands as written and
cannot be edited.

{payload}

Disruption-content query tools (layer L2) are now available to you, in
addition to every tool you already had.

In operations, a disruption calls for a prompt response: revise your
delivery plan with the information at hand. When you are ready, submit a
complete report of type "revision" through the submission tool. Its
revision log lists every claim whose status changed relative to your plan
report, and its plan section carries your full revised route plan.

The log is checked against your saved plan report at save time: a claim
you carry over keeps its id (log it "modified" if you changed its
content, or leave it out of the log if unchanged); a claim you drop is
logged "retired" under its original id; only genuinely new claims are
logged "added". A log that contradicts your saved plan report is
rejected.

mcp.docstring:
mcp_server — the harness tool surface as an MCP server over stdio (plan step 4).

Plan "Creating a general geospatial harness", step 4 (2026-10-10). The
receipt gate (`layer_tools._serve`: grants check, execute, store the payload
under its r-id, write the tool_log line, hand back the view) is unchanged
and sits behind every tool here: a call over stdio and the same call made
in-process by the lin and self topologies mint receipts into the same run
folder, under the same cross-process lock, and leave identical ledgers.

THE SURFACE IS CANONICAL. `canonical_tools(granted)` is the one list of
tools a run offers under a grant set and the current flags: the names are
`layer_tools.tools_for_layers`, each description is the core's docstring
exactly as `render_tool_docs` prints it, and each input schema is derived
from the core's own signature. The server's list_tools answers from this
function on every request, reading the run's grants file each time, so the
surface grows at each unlock exactly as the in-process surface does.
test_mcp_parity asserts the in-process list and the stdio list are
byte-identical for every grant set and flag state.

RUN CONTEXT comes from the environment the server inherits, as it does for
every in-process caller: DOE_MAS_RUN_DIR (the run folder with grants.json,
tool_log.jsonl and tool_results/), DOE_MAS_DB, DOE_MAS_REGISTRY_DIR, the
DOE_MAS_OKF / DOE_MAS_REPORT_TOOLS flags and DOE_MAS_SUBMITTING_STAGE
(finalize_report is on the surface only while it is "1").

CLI:
    DOE_MAS_RUN_DIR=/path/to/run python3 -m agentic_harness_workflow.mcp_server
Clients: agentic_harness_workflow.mcp_client (sync, for tests and executors)
or any MCP client speaking stdio.
mcp.main:
def main(argv=None) -> int:
    import argparse
    import asyncio
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    ap.add_argument("--list", action="store_true",
                    help="print the canonical tool list for the current run context and exit")
    args = ap.parse_args(argv)
    if args.list:
        print(json.dumps(canonical_tools(), indent=1))
        return 0
    run_dir = os.environ.get("DOE_MAS_RUN_DIR")
    if not run_dir or not Path(run_dir).is_dir():
        print("mcp_server: DOE_MAS_RUN_DIR must name the run folder", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    asyncio.run(_serve_stdio())
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

data_guide_html:
Network data guide (reference)

The working copy is a spatial graph of Alaska's fuel network, reached only through the tools. describe() renders its shape from the database itself: every relation with columns and row counts, the modes, the months and the id kinds. In brief:

  • Nodes are places on the network. Some are hubs: bulk-fuel staging points with tank capacity, delivery methods and a community name.
  • Edges connect nodes, about 93,000 of them, each weighted for every month x mode (road, barge, plane, ice_road, transfer) with friction, cost and passability. Ice roads pass only in winter, barge only in open water. Transfer edges are where fuel changes carrier.
  • Facilities are the ~1,800 delivery endpoints. Each maps to the hub that serves it, with a last_mile of local or remote; about 100 remote sites sit more than 25 km from their staging hub, and reaching the hub does not deliver them.
  • Communities are names, not ids. resolve turns a name into the hubs that share it, against the authoritative Alaska community list.

What the numbers mean

Edge weights are modelled, not observed prices. Each edge's monthly avg_friction is derived from environmental surfaces (river and sea ice, permafrost, slope, land cover). An edge's cost_per_gallon is already integrated over its length: miles x friction x the mode's per-gallon-mile rate, or a flat intermodal fee on a transfer edge. Summing a route's segment costs gives its total cost per gallon, and the cheapest path per gallon is the routing objective; the shortest path is a diagnostic. nodata_frac reports how much of an edge's friction surface lacked data: uncertainty worth a claim, not a fact. Passability is computed per month x mode from the same surfaces; an impassable edge-month has no weight.

This working copy is the authoritative world for your task. Where your general knowledge of Alaska and the data disagree, the data governs, and places or connections you expect to exist count only if the tools return them.
report_format_html:
Report format (reference)

The report is one JSON object with exactly these six top-level keys and no others: meta, summary, plan, coverage, claims, revision (the harness alone adds a seventh, segments_sidecar, when it saves the report). No section may be omitted; any section may be empty. No object anywhere in the report may carry keys beyond those listed here.

meta: {"schema_version": "0.4.0", "report_type": "<type>"} where <type> is plan, revision, or reassessment.

summary: a string. May be empty.

plan: {"routes": [...]}. One route is one delivery. Each route object has exactly: - route_id: "rt-" + three digits, e.g. "rt-001"; unique per report - legs: a non-empty list of leg objects, in the order they happen - facilities_served: a list of strings, each "facility:<public id>"

Each leg object has exactly: - mode: one of "road", "barge", "plane", "ice_road", "transfer". A transfer is a real movement — fuel changing carrier at a dock, port or airstrip — with its own edges, months and cost. Legs split at mode changes, so a barge delivery that lands and transfers is at least two legs - months: {"start": M, "end": M} — integers 1–12 (wrap-around allowed) - segments: on a leg you type, a non-empty list of strings, each "edge:<public id>", listed in the order they are travelled — first edge first, last edge last - from_receipt, receipt_leg, n_edges, first_edge, last_edge (written by the harness, never by you): a leg committed by reference — add_route legs=[{"from_receipt": "r-####", "leg": n, ...}] — is stored as this summary instead of its segments; the harness may add length_km, cost_per_gallon, from_node, to_node and tiles_r5 (the H3 cells the leg crosses, in order) from the receipt. Its edge ids stay the commitment: at finalize the harness writes every leg's ids beside the saved report (report_<type>.segments.json, named by the top-level segments_sidecar) and the scorers read them from there - via_corridors (optional): ["corridor:<public id>", ...] — provenance for where the segments came from, when a concept-map corridor page supplied them. It never replaces the edges: they are the commitment, the corridors are the citation trail

A delivery that uses one mode from start to finish is a route with one leg. A delivery that changes mode part way is one route with a leg per mode, each leg carrying its own months: legs of one delivery need not run in the same season, and the gap between one leg's end and the next leg's start is fuel held in storage. Whether two movements are one delivery or two separate routes is your judgement.

coverage: {"facilities_served": [...], "facilities_unserved": [...]} — both lists of "facility:<public id>" strings; either may be empty. An optional third key, facilities_remote_declared, lists remote facilities (more than 25 km from their staging hub, last_mile "remote" in lookup(kind="hub_facility_map")) supplied from a hub a route reaches by an off-network leg the data does not contain. Each entry is {"facility": "facility:<id>", "staging_hub": "hub:<id>", "last_mile_mode": <one of plane, helicopter, landing_craft, snowmachine, truck, other>, "note": "<optional, ≤400 chars>"}. Declared deliveries are counted apart from coverage, never as served; a remote facility in facilities_served is a misclaim. expanded_from_hubs (optional, written by the harness) records which coverage entries were expanded from a hub id given to set_coverage; the lists still hold every facility.

claims: a list of claim objects. Each has exactly: - id: "c-" + four digits, e.g. "c-0001"; unique per report - class: "sourced" or "inferred" - section: one of "route_design", "disruption_response", "ancillary_context", "risk_outlook", "recommendation" — use "recommendation" for an action that is not itself a delivery. Sections record information that has actually reached you this run: write "disruption_response" only when a disruption notice has been delivered — if none has, leave that section unused rather than inferring or anticipating one, and likewise "ancillary_context" carries context that was delivered or retrieved, not imagined. An empty section is the correct record of an information state, not a gap to fill - text: a non-empty string - refs: a list (may be empty) of strings, each "<prefix>:<id>" with prefix one of edge, node, facility, hub, route, corridor, window, assumption. For edge, node, facility, and hub the <id> is a public id copied from a tool result; route names a route_id in this report; corridor, window, and assumption are your own labels for constructs of your analysis - if class is "sourced": additionally cites — a non-empty list of retrieval ids "r-" + four digits — and NO derives_from key - if class is "inferred": additionally derives_from — a non-empty list of claim ids that appear in this report's claims — and NO cites key

revision: {"log": [...]}. Each log entry has exactly claim_id ("c-" + four digits), action ("modified", "retired", or "added"), and rationale_claims (a list of claim ids, may be empty). When report_type is plan the log MUST be empty. In a revision report the log records changes relative to the saved plan report; in a reassessment report, relative to the saved revision report.

Claim ids persist across the run's reports: a claim carried over from your previous report KEEPS its id (with action: "modified" in the log if its content changed, or no log entry if unchanged); a claim from the previous report that no longer holds is logged "retired" under its original id; a claim new in this report gets a new id and is logged "added". The same persistence applies to route_ids.

Where ids come from. A public id is the id a data tool returned: facilities look like facility:f000139, edges like edge:e068363, hubs like hub:h000319, nodes like node:n053223. Copy them verbatim from tool results — an element's id exists only in the data, so every facility, edge, hub, and node id you write must appear in the result of a tool call you made this run. If you could not retrieve an element's id, do not construct one: describe the element in a claim's text and mark that claim inferred, or record the delivery at the level you did retrieve (a hub, a region) rather than inventing the missing detail. Ids and labels use letters, digits, _, ., - only. Format the report JSON across multiple lines with indentation — it need not be one line, and line breaks make a large report easier to close correctly.

The save tool enforces this against your previously saved report: logging an existing claim as "added", dropping a claim without a "retired" entry, or changing a claim without a "modified" entry is rejected, with each mismatch listed.

glossary.meaning: One invocation of the runner: a seeded plan of runs, executed together. One folder here.
One team working one task from start to finish, saving one to three reports. One `runs/<run>_<topology>/` folder.

How the agents are organised. `lin`: a fixed sequence of stages, the reference. `self`: a planner agent designs its own team, which then runs in dependency order. `crew`: a team of named roles (CrewAI) whose analysts hand their work to a report writer. `mass`: parallel peers work independently and vote; the winner's report is submitted (MassGen).

The routing task: `statewide_annual_v1` (the whole state, one annual cycle) or `bering_straits_annual_v1` (Anchorage to the 20 Bering Straits hubs, one annual cycle). `unspecified` marks the first pilot, which predates the scenario files.

A point where a run saves a report. `plan`: routes and coverage with the network. `revision`: the plan revised after a disruption notice. `reassessment`: the plan reassessed after the context documents arrive.
What a run may use from the start. `L1`: the network only. `L1+L2`: the network and a disruption notice. Layers are granted by the harness, never by an agent.
A run with information set `L1` whose disruption is delivered after the plan; it saves plan, revision and reassessment.
A run given the disruption notice at the start (`L1+L2`); it saves one plan.
The break the harness applies. `D2`: storm damage closes the Nome fuel hub for the season. Every arm here uses D2; `D1` and `D3` are defined in `agentic_harness_workflow/disruptions/`.
The budget ceilings in force. `treatment`: the original caps (every arm before 2026-10-21). `fuse`: caps raised to ceilings no honest run should reach, the default since 2026-10-21.
The `r-####` id every data-tool call returns. A report's claims cite receipts, and the scorers check them against the run's tool log.
A model that scores each report on five dimensions (reasoning support, operational coherence, evidence engagement, change discipline, calibrated honesty), 0 to 4, without knowing the topology.
The run saved every report it owed and passed the save gate each time.

key_terms.meaning: How a team of agents is organised. `lin`: a fixed sequence of stages (the reference). `crew`: a team of named roles (CrewAI). `mass`: parallel peers that vote (MassGen). `self`: a planner agent designs its own team at run time.
The routing problem a run is given: between two named hubs (`pair`), within named regions (`region`), or across the whole state (`statewide`).
What a team may query. **L1**: the network, friction surface, routes and costs. **L2**: a disruption. **L3**: socio-economic context documents. Access is granted by the harness, never by an agent.

The two halves of the study design. In the **factorial arm** each run starts cold with a fixed set of layers and writes one plan. In the **progressive arm** a run writes a plan with L1, then receives a disruption (L2) and writes a revision, then receives context (L3) and writes a reassessment.
One combination of scenario, topology, arm, information set and disruption. Each run belongs to one cell.
A point where a run saves a report: plan, revision, reassessment.
Everything a run sees: instruction text, tools, model settings, budgets. It is identical across topologies except for each topology's short adapter.

The three freeze levels of the treatment surface: **frozen** artifacts (schemas, tools, scenarios, scorers) never change once frozen; **shared** instructions are delivered word-for-word to every topology; **adapters** are the one short per-topology text, limited to describing the agent's position.
The `r-####` id every data-tool call returns. Report claims cite it, and graders check it against the run's tool log.
A disruption's hidden answer key: the network elements it affects.
An environment variable that switches a support feature (skills, concept map, report tools) off, to measure its effect.
